evidence.claim: Granite tunnels and climbing bridges shape a road built for slow sightseeing
evidence.quote: The road, like several other scenic roads in the Black Hills, was originally laid out by Governor Peter Norbeck, specifically to create a very scenic, slow-speed road for tourists.

evidence.claim: Granite tunnels and climbing bridges

evidence.claim: The Peter Norbeck Scenic Byway threads the Black Hills through rock tunnels, across spiraling bridges and among granite pinnacles and pine-covered mountains.
evidence.quote: it winds its way around spiraling "pig-tail" shaped bridges, through six rock tunnels, among towering granite pinnacles and over pristine, pine-clad mountains.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway as 68 miles and allows four hours to drive it.
evidence.quote: Peter Norbeck Scenic Byway National Scenic Byway • South Dakota Length 68.0 mi / 109.4 km Time to Allow Allow four hours to drive the byway

evidence.claim: The Forest Service highlights Mount Rushmore, Custer State Park, Needles Highway and Iron Mountain Road along the route.
evidence.quote: The Peter Norbeck Scenic Byway offers 70 miles of sights including the National Forest, Mount Rushmore, Needles Highway, Iron Mountain Rd & Custer State Park.

evidence.claim: On the Needles Highway, that landscape includes ponderosa pine and Black Hills spruce forests, with birch and aspen surrounding the meadows.
evidence.quote: ponderosa pine and Black Hills spruce forests, meadows surrounded by birch and aspen, and rugged granite mountains.

evidence.claim: Peter Norbeck planned the Needles Highway by marking its course on foot and horseback; construction finished in 1922.
evidence.quote: The roadway was carefully planned by former South Dakota Governor Peter Norbeck, who marked the entire course on foot and by horseback. Construction was completed in 1922.

evidence.claim: He then chose the layout of Iron Mountain Road in the 1930s and pressed ahead despite being told it could not be built.
evidence.quote: In the 1930s, he chose the layout of the Iron Mountain Road and persisted in building it, even after being told his vision was impossible

evidence.claim: Its three tunnels frame Mount Rushmore, while pigtail bridges let the road gain or lose height quickly.
evidence.quote: including three tunnels that frame Mount Rushmore in the distance. The road is famous for the "Pigtail Bridges" that allow travelers to drop or gain altitude quickly.

evidence.claim: The scenic byway was established in his honor on September 23, 1996.
evidence.quote: The byway was established on September 23, 1996, and named in honor of Norbeck.

evidence.claim: For a circuit from Custer, take U.S. 16A east through Custer State Park, then follow Iron Mountain Road toward Keystone.
evidence.quote: The byway enters Custer State Park along its eastern edge and turns west at its intersection with SD 36.

evidence.claim: then follow Iron Mountain Road toward Keystone.
evidence.quote: The byway is part of US 16A, the Iron Mountain Road, south of Keystone.

evidence.claim: South Dakota 244 leads west past Mount Rushmore; connect to SD 87 for the return toward Sylvan Lake.
evidence.quote: The byway then follows SD 87 to its intersection with US 16 and US 385, where it becomes part of the nearby SD 244. The byway follows SD 244 eastward into the Mount Rushmore National Memorial, where it meets up with US 16A.
